We prove both set inclusions, as required by a double inclusion proof. If x∈A∖(B∪C), then x∈A and x∈/B∪C. Thus x∈/B and x∈/C, so x∈A∖B and x∈A∖C. This proves the forward set inclusion.
Conversely, if x∈(A∖B)∩(A∖C), then x∈A, x∈/B, and x∈/C. Hence x∈/B∪C, giving x∈A∖(B∪C). Therefore
A∖(B∪C)=(A∖B)∩(A∖C).​
(1)

ii OurBigBook.com
For the first set inclusion, take x∈(A∩B)∖C. Membership in the intersection gives x∈A and x∈B, while the set difference gives x∈/C. Consequently x∈(A∖C)∩(B∖C).
For the reverse set inclusion, an element of (A∖C)∩(B∖C) belongs to both A and B and does not belong to C. It therefore belongs to (A∩B)∖C. By double inclusion proof,
(A∩B)∖C=(A∖C)∩(B∖C).​
(2)

Complements are relative to the same universal set U. Suppose A⊆B and x∈B. Then x∈U and x∈/B. If x belonged to A, the assumed set inclusion would imply x∈B, a contradiction. Thus x∈/A and x∈A, proving
A⊆B ⟹ B⊆A.​
(3)
There is only one set inclusion in this conclusion; a reverse inclusion is neither needed nor generally true. The request for double inclusion applies to the equalities in (i) and (ii).

i OurBigBook.com
Fix one distinguished element a of the n-element set. Every partition of a set into l blocks belongs to exactly one of two cases. If {a} is a block, removing it leaves an (l−1)-block partition of a set of the other n−1 elements, giving S(n−1,l−1) possibilities. Otherwise remove a from its block; that block remains nonempty, so the result has l blocks. Conversely choose any of the S(n−1,l) such partitions and insert a in any one of its l blocks. This gives lS(n−1,l) possibilities.
These cases are disjoint and exhaustive, proving the Stirling numbers of the second kind recurrence
S(n,l)=lS(n−1,l)+S(n−1,l−1).​
(9)
Use S(0,0)=1, S(n,0)=0 for n>0, and S(n,l)=0 for l>n; these conventions include the boundary cases n=1 and l=1.

Solution
Words: 81
ii OurBigBook.com
Starting from n singleton blocks, a partition of a set into n−1 nonempty blocks has exactly one block of size two and all other blocks of size one: the sum of the block sizes exceeds the number of blocks by exactly one. Choosing that pair determines the partition uniquely. Hence
S(n,n−1)=(2n​),k=2.​
(10)
This fixed value of k works for every n≥2. It is forced already by n=2: S(2,1)=1, whereas for positive k the only (k2​) equal to one is (22​).

a OurBigBook.com
Count pairs (M,K) of subsets of an n-element candidate set with K⊆M, ∣M∣=m, and ∣K∣=k. Choosing the whole team M first and then the special-role players K gives (mn​)(km​). Alternatively choose K first, then choose the other m−k players from the n−k candidates outside K, giving (kn​)(m−kn−k​). Each construction specifies the same pair uniquely. Thus double counting proves
(mn​)(km​)=(kn​)(m−kn−k​).​
(14)

Using the wiki convention that paths follow the written order of the binary relations, composition of relations is
R∘S={(x,z)∈A×A:∃y∈A, (x,y)∈R and (y,z)∈S}.​

Some treatments reverse the naming convention; stating it explicitly avoids ambiguity. The powers of the single relation R below are the same under either convention.

Solution
Words: 47
ii OurBigBook.com
A pair belongs to R∘R exactly when two successive R steps connect its endpoints. The chain a→b→c→d has two such length-two paths, a→b→c and b→c→d. Hence
R∘R={(a,c),(b,d)}.​
(16)
This applies composition of relations directly; no other middle element gives a pair.

Words: 81 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 81
iii OurBigBook.com
The relation powers are R2={(a,c),(b,d)}, R3={(a,d)}, and Ri=∅ for i≥4. For k=1, (a,b),(b,c)∈T but (a,c)∈/T, so transitivity fails. For k=2, (a,c),(c,d)∈T but (a,d)∈/T, so it still fails.
For k=3, T consists of every pair in which the first endpoint precedes the second in a,b,c,d. Composing any two such pairs again gives such a pair, so T is transitive. Thus the smallest k is 3; this T is the transitive closure of a relation R.

In the partially ordered set (A,⪯), the assertion m=lub(S) means both
(∀s∈S, s⪯m)and(∀u∈A, [∀s∈S, s⪯u]⇒m⪯u).​
(17)
The first condition makes m an upper bound; the second makes it the least upper bound. Both conditions are necessary, and antisymmetry makes such an element unique.

ii

Words: 101 Articles: 1
c OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 101
ii OurBigBook.com
Suppose m is the greatest lower bound of the set X of all upper bounds of S. Every s∈S satisfies s⪯x for every x∈X, so each such s is a lower bound of X. Since m is the greatest of those lower bounds, s⪯m for every s∈S. Thus m itself is an upper bound of S, meaning m∈X.
Also m, being a lower bound of X, satisfies m⪯x for every x∈X. It is therefore an upper bound of S below every other upper bound, which proves m=lub(S). The argument also covers empty S or X whenever the assumed greatest lower bound exists.

We prove the contrapositive. If 3∤a, Euclidean division gives a=3q+1 or a=3q+2 for an integer q. Squaring gives respectively a2=3(3q2+2q)+1 or a2=3(3q2+4q+1)+1. Both have remainder 1 upon division by 3, so 3∤a2. Taking the contrapositive yields 3∣a2⇒3∣a.

b OurBigBook.com
For a proof by contradiction, suppose 3​=a/b for positive integers a,b in lowest terms, so gcd(a,b)=1. Squaring gives a2=3b2, and part (a) implies 3∣a. Write a=3c; then 9c2=3b2, hence b2=3c2, and part (a) again implies 3∣b. This contradicts the coprimality of a,b. Therefore 3​ is an irrational number.

Solution

Words: 46
c OurBigBook.com
The fifty disjoint sets {1,100},{2,99},…,{50,51} form a partition of a set {1,…,100}. If a chosen subset met each pair at most once, it would contain at most fifty elements. The pigeonhole principle therefore forces a 51-element subset to contain both elements of at least one pair. Those two distinct elements sum to 101.

Assume n≥1 and list the elements of X as a1​,…,an​. Define the partial sums sj​=a1​+⋯+aj​ for 1≤j≤n. If one is divisible by n, its corresponding nonempty prefix is a suitable Y.
Otherwise the n partial sums have remainders in the n−1 nonzero residue classes. The pigeonhole principle gives i<j with si​≡sj​(modn). Thus sj​−si​=ai+1​+⋯+aj​ is divisible by n, giving a nonempty subset Y={ai+1​,…,aj​}.
Therefore a nonempty Y exists. This strengthens the literal assertion, which would otherwise allow the trivial empty set with sum zero.

Prove the explicit bound n!≤2n2 by mathematical induction. At n=1, 1≤2. For the step, note that n+1≤2n for n≥1: this auxiliary inequality has base 2=2 and follows at the next index from n+2≤2(n+1). Hence, using the induction hypothesis,
(n+1)!≤(n+1)2n2≤2n2+n≤2(n+1)2.
(20)
Thus n!=O((2n)n), with constant 1 and threshold 1 in big O notation.

Solution
Words: 66
ii OurBigBook.com
We prove the stronger explicit bound n!≤nn/2n−1 by mathematical induction. The case n=1 is equality. The binomial theorem gives (1+1/n)n≥1+n/n=2, so (n+1)n≥2nn. Consequently the induction hypothesis yields
(n+1)!≤2n−1(n+1)nn​≤2n(n+1)n+1​.
(21)
Therefore n!=O(nn/2n), with constant 2 and threshold 1.
The second bound is asymptotically tighter. Using n≤2n,
2n2nn/2n​=(2n+1n​)n≤2−n⟶0.
(22)
Thus its bounding function is negligible relative to the first in little o notation; this compares the bounds without needing Stirling's formula.

The characteristic equation of a constant-coefficient differential equation here is r2−3r+2=(r−1)(r−2)=0. Its homogeneous solution is C1​ex+C2​e2x. Because the forcing ex is already a homogeneous mode, the method of undetermined coefficients requires yp​=Axex rather than Aex.
Here yp′​=A(x+1)ex and yp′′​=A(x+2)ex, so yp′′​−3yp′​+2yp​=−Aex. Thus A=−1, and the general solution is
y(x)=C1​ex+C2​e2x−xex.​

The gradient vanishes when 4x+3y−1=0 and 3x+2y−1=0. Subtracting these equations gives x+y=0, so the unique critical point is (x,y)=(1,−1)​, with f(1,−1)=0.
The Hessian matrix is
H=(43​32​),detH=8−9=−1<0.
(26)
It is indefinite, so the critical point is a saddle point. Explicitly, around that point the change is exactly 2u2+3uv+v2: it is positive for v=0,u=0 and negative for v=−3u/2,u=0. Thus arbitrarily close points have both larger and smaller values.

On the unit circle the constraint gradient (2x,2y) never vanishes. The Lagrange multiplier equations are
8x−3y=2λx,−3x=2λy,x2+y2=1.
(27)
A nonzero solution of the first two equations requires
det(8−2λ−3​−3−2λ​)=4λ2−16λ−9=0,
(28)
so λ=9/2 or λ=−1/2. Multiplying the first equation by x, the second by y, and adding shows 2f=2λ(x2+y2)=2λ. Thus each candidate value of f equals its multiplier.
For λ=9/2, y=−x/3, giving (x,y)=±(3,−1)/10​. For λ=−1/2, y=3x, giving (x,y)=±(1,3)/10​. Since a continuous function attains its extrema on the compact set given by the unit circle and these exhaust the Lagrange multiplier candidates,
fmax​=29​ at ±10​(3,−1)​,fmin​=−21​ at ±10​(1,3)​.​
(29)
Each ± changes both coordinates together.

For the Fourier sine series write u0​(x)=∑n≥1​bn​sin(nπx/L). Orthogonality of trigonometric functions gives
bn​=L2​∫0L​u0​(x)sinLnπx​dx.
(32)
In the second half of the integral put z=L−x; then u0​(L−z)=ρz and sin[nπ(L−z)/L]=(−1)n+1sin(nπz/L). Hence
bn​=L2ρ​[1+(−1)n+1]∫0L/2​xsinLnπx​dx.
(33)
Every even coefficient is zero. For odd n, part (a) or the supplied integral yields
bn​=n2π24Lρ​sin2nπ​.
(34)
Putting n=2m+1 therefore gives
u0​(x)=m=0∑∞​Fm​sinL(2m+1)πx​,Fm​=(−1)m(2m+1)2π24Lρ​.​
(35)
This is the Fourier sine series of a symmetric tent. The absolute values of its terms are uniformly bounded by a summable sequence, giving absolute convergence and uniform convergence; the piecewise smooth odd extension and the Dirichlet convergence theorem for Fourier series identify its value with the continuous u0​, including the zero endpoints and the peak.
The printed lower limit m=1 is an error. The original PDF visibly has this lower limit. It omits the nonzero fundamental coefficient F0​=4Lρ/π2. In particular, the printed series equals u0​(x)−F0​sin(πx/L), rather than u0​(x). At x=L/2 it gives Lρ/2−4Lρ/π2 instead of Lρ/2. The corrected lower limit is displayed explicitly above.

c OurBigBook.com
Apply separation of variables to each mode of the damped wave equation utt​+2k2ut​=c2uxx​, assuming L,c>0. The spatial ordinary differential equation is Xn′′​+(λn​/c)2Xn​=0. Its general solution is Csin(λn​x/c)+Dcos(λn​x/c). The boundary condition at 0 gives D=0; a nonzero mode at L requires
λn​=Lnπc​,n=1,2,…,Xn​(x)=sinLnπx​.​
(36)
Only odd n=2m+1 occur in the initial Fourier sine series. Put ωm​=(2m+1)πc/L and dm​=k4−ωm2​​. The temporal equation Tm′′​+2k2Tm′​+ωm2​Tm​=0 has roots −k2±dm​. Define
αm​=k2−dm​,βm​=k2+dm​.​
(37)
For distinct roots, let the full amplitude be qm​(t)=Am​e−αm​t+Bm​e−βm​t. The initial displacement and zero initial velocity impose Am​+Bm​=Fm​ and αm​Am​+βm​Bm​=0. Solving gives
Am​=βm​−αm​βm​Fm​​,Bm​=−βm​−αm​αm​Fm​​.​
(38)
Thus the physically consistent superposition is
u(x,t)=m=0∑∞​qm​(t)sinL(2m+1)πx​.​
(39)
For ωm​<k2 there is overdamping, with two real decaying exponentials. For ωm​>k2 there is underdamping; set νm​=ωm2​−k4​; the equivalent real expression is
qm​(t)=Fm​e−k2t(cos(νm​t)+νm​k2​sin(νm​t)).
(40)
At critical damping, the repeated-root case ωm​=k2, take the limit, giving qm​(t)=Fm​(1+k2t)e−k2t. These formulas all satisfy qm​(0)=Fm​ and qm′​(0)=0.
Three source qualifications matter. First, the sum must start at m=0, for the same reason as in (b). Second, the printed X(x)=u0​(x) cannot hold for a single separated mode: the tent has X′′=0 on each open linear segment but X=0, contradicting X′′=−(λn​/c)2X for positive λn​, and its peak is not twice differentiable. Separation applies mode by mode, with the initial tent recovered by superposition. Third, no finite “large” k makes every mode overdamped, because ωm​→∞. The two-exponential expression permits complex conjugate roots, while a repeated root requires its displayed limiting form. The tent initial data are naturally interpreted through the convergent modal solution, rather than as a single smooth separated product.

A further use of “midpoint” is the two-step explicit midpoint linear multistep method, yi+1​=yi−1​+2hΦ(xi​,yi​), which needs a second starting value. Put h=(b−a)/n, gi​=g(xi​), and z0​=0. Under the endpoint-slope convention suggested by the requested connection, the recurrence is zi+1​=zi​+2h​(gi​+gi+1​). Summing telescopes, so
zn​=nb−a​[2g0​+gn​​+i=1∑n−1​gi​]=Tn​(g).​
(49)
Since G(b)=∫ab​g(x)dx by the fundamental theorem of calculus, this recurrence gives exactly the composite trapezoidal rule. It replaces the average derivative over each strip by the arithmetic mean of its endpoint derivatives.
For the standard midpoint method, the literal endpoint-only request is not valid for general g. Both the explicit and implicit one-step midpoint formulas here give instead
zn​=hi=0∑n−1​g(xi​+h/2)=Mn​(g),​
(50)
the composite midpoint quadrature rule. It requires half-grid samples. These samples cannot be recovered exactly from g0​,…,gn​ for arbitrary smooth g: the zero function and g(x)=∏j=0n​(x−xj​)2 have identical grid values but different midpoint sums. For a smooth g, replacing each half-grid sample by (gi​+gi+1​)/2 is an additional approximation, giving Tn​ with an O(h2) total difference, rather than an identity. A precise useful relation, obtained by splitting the finer trapezoidal sum into old nodes and midpoints, is
T2n​(g)=21​[Tn​(g)+Mn​(g)],Mn​(g)=2T2n​(g)−Tn​(g).​
(51)
Here T2n​ uses the finer half-grid, so it does not eliminate the missing data.
If “Mid-Point Method” means the two-step explicit midpoint linear multistep method, the recurrence is zi+1​=zi−1​+2hgi​. It gives z2r​=2h∑j=1r​g2j−1​ and z2r+1​=z1​+2h∑j=1r​g2j​, so an odd final index additionally needs a starting value z1​. For even n=2r, the result is the midpoint quadrature on r double-width strips; equivalently zn​=2Tn​−Tn/2​. The question specifies neither even n nor a starter. Thus the trapezoidal expression above is the natural endpoint-average interpretation, while the other common midpoint meanings require the qualifications just given. The ambiguity is present in the original PDF.

P(Sn​=k)=(kn​)pk(1−p)n−k,k=0,…,n.​

Choose the k successful events in (kn​) ways; independence gives the same product probability for each choice. At p=0 or p=1, interpret the formula by its degenerate distribution or by continuity.
